scope: Out-of-period validation case for a bounded, predominantly local-food horticultural island system; not a 1337 training target.

promotion_audit.decision: Retain as validation-only. Brown and Crema provide relative archaeological population trajectories and support logistic leveling in the northern horticultural zone around AD 1500, but do not provide a defensible absolute population interval for the North Island at 1337. Late-contact whole-New-Zealand estimates are retained only as a clearly separated reference range.

records.label: Northern Aotearoa Māori horticultural-zone population-pressure validation
records.reference_population_interval_date: late pre-contact/1769 literature synthesis; not assigned to 1450-1500
records.interval_semantics: No absolute 1450-1500 North Island population interval is admitted. The 90,000-150,000 reference range comes from late-contact/late pre-contact syntheses and cannot be projected backward into the target year without an audited demographic model.
pressure_evidence: Brown and Crema (2021), pp. 580-586, use summed radiocarbon-date probabilities and archaeological site frequencies to show strong spatially heterogeneous population growth, with the northern horticultural zone following a logistic pattern and leveling around AD 1500.

Brown and Crema (2021), pp. 584-586, identify the northern half of the North Island as the optimal horticultural environment, with growth hotspots in Western Bay of Plenty, Waikato and Auckland and a reduction of growth as carrying capacity was approached.

Te Ara's environmental synthesis records rapid Māori deforestation, fire-driven land conversion and depletion of large fauna after settlement; these are independent local resource-pressure signals, not population labels.
Kumara horticulture, storage pits, fishing and shellfish exploitation are documented in the archaeological literature; crops were concentrated in warmer North Island environments.
shock_flags: inter-tribal movement and warfare are not resolved at island scale
records.trade_dependence: low_to_mixed for staple calories; horticulture, fishing and foraging were local, with inter-island exchange and chiefly redistribution not quantified
records.boundary_description: North Island (Te Ika-a-Māui), excluding South Island, Stewart Island and the Chatham Islands. This is a mappable island boundary used as a proxy for the warmer northern horticultural zone; the archaeological study's regional bins are not identical to the island polygon.
records.boundary_source: Stats NZ/official island geography; Brown and Crema (2021), Figure 2 regional sampling; Te Ara environmental history
records.boundary_confidence: high for island polygon; medium for equivalence to archaeological northern zone
records.source_family_independence: Brown and Crema's radiocarbon/site-frequency model and the environmental/settlement syntheses are related archaeological evidence but are treated as one New Zealand validation family.
citation_details: Brown and Crema (2021), pp. 580-586: Northern New Zealand logistic population trajectory and leveling around AD 1500; pp. 584-585 explicitly caution that absolute density is difficult because population projections have weak empirical bases.
Te Ara, Human effects on the environment: rapid post-settlement deforestation, fire and loss of large fauna.
Te Ara, Taupori Māori: Cook's 1769 estimate of 100,000 and feasible-growth context; retained only as late-contact reference, not a 1337 target.
records.notes: Useful hostile/ordinary island food-system stress test with strong local-food and pressure evidence. It must not be promoted to training until an absolute population series and exact archaeological northern-zone boundary are independently reconstructed. No starting-population field, HYDE field, RGO output modifier or regional correction is used.
